newsitem.title: ITALY: Van Miert to seek assurance in Italy on Iri debt.
newsitem.headline: Van Miert to seek assurance in Italy on Iri debt.

text.p: European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said at the weekend he would seek assurances from Italy on what it planed to do over the likely failure of state industrial holding Iri to cut its debt by the end of the year.

Under a 1993 agreement between Italy and the Commission, IRI must cut its debt of 25 trillion lire to below 5.0 trillion lire ($3.3 billion) by the end of 1996 with the possibility of an extension if justified by the market situation.
Van Miert, at this lakeside resort for a business forum, said: "It seems some of the commitments which had been taken will not be realised in due time, so this has to be discussed."

Van Miert will visit Rome from Monday to discuss the matter. He will meet Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi, Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi and Posts Minister Antonio Maccanico during his two-day visit.
"There should be no doubt that the process should go on in due time and this will be the aim of the discussion," he told reporters.
Part of Iri's problem has been that the privatisation of state telecommunications holding Stet, of which IRI holds 47 percent, has been delayed.

The sell off is now slated for February or March next year but the government has yet to get legislation establishing a regulator for the telecoms sector through parliament. A watchdog is a prerequisite for Stet's privatisation.

Asked if the delays to Stet's privatisation would influence the Commission's position, Van Miert said he wanted to know as precisely as possible what the government intended to do in the coming weeks and months.
"Secondly, then within the framework of our responsibility I want to see how far we can push to make sure what has been agreed will be realised," he said.

"It wasn't easy at the time to convince other members of the Commission or other member states that this two-year period was absolutely needed. Now it appears that more time is needed so we must have a very good explanation if we go beyond the end of the year," he said.

He declined to discuss what he planned to say to the government and noted it was up to Rome to find ways and means and not up to the Commission to impose these. He said he would "eventually" have suggestions as to what the government should do, "but that will be just friendly advice".
